meaning.evidence: Every beat survives: the bald question, the portrait, the reading list, the four books, the $1.12, the geometry report, the holidays, the telegram P.S. Small rewordings keep sense: "and pretty well, too" for "very satisfactorily", "pick up without trying" for "know by absorption", "there's another Freshman from Texas staying back too".

sense.evidence: Each swap fits: "a verandah roof" for porch roof, "You're a crabby old thing with a temper on you" for snappy, "so chock-a-block you can hardly get through" for cluttered, "what she's on about" for talking about, "Hooroo, Daddy" as the sign-off.

authenticity.evidence: The Aussie is natural and unforced: "I've got four on the go at once", "If you can't be bothered writing", "I haven't told anybody, mind". One clumsy line: "a sort of sprinkly grey sort of hair".

register.evidence: A light level-2 touch, clean throughout: "verandah", "chock-a-block", "on the go", "Hooroo", with the letter's voice left intact; no swearing.

tone.evidence: Judy's eager, playful voice stays: "Oh, you see, I know!", "And oh, it's fun!", the mock-formal "I have the honour to report fresh explorations in the field of geometry."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly, apart from the doubled "a sort of sprinkly grey sort of hair" and the slightly wordy "the study's getting left by the wayside".

variety.evidence: Different terms each time: "verandah", "crabby", "on the go", "chock-a-block", "Hooroo", "on about"; the closing "Bye till January" avoids repeating Hooroo.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the Daddy-Long-Legs letter, its shape of dated entries and interruptions kept: "(Ten o'clock bell. This is a very interrupted letter.)"

problems.quote: a sort of sprinkly grey sort of hair
the study's getting left by the wayside
problems.why: "the study" reads as a room; slightly awkward.

A.summary: A light, natural level-2 retelling that keeps every point and Judy's voice; one clumsy doubled phrase.

meaning.evidence: All points kept; one added opener, "Ya won't believe this, but you never answered my question", is colour rather than new fact. Otherwise close: "there's another Freshman who lives in Texas staying back too".

sense.evidence: Most terms fit: "so chockers you can hardly get through", "a beaut time over the holidays", "heaps of others besides". "and a merry Chrissie!" strains: Chrissie is used in compounds, not usually in the greeting.

authenticity.evidence: Natural in places ("I've got four on the go at once", "cos there are eighteen blank years behind me"), but the bolted-on "Ya won't believe this" and "merry Chrissie" read as pastiche.

register.evidence: Slightly above a light touch with "Ya", "cos", "chockers", "beaut", "Hooroo" twice and "Chrissie"; still clean, near level 2.

tone.evidence: Mostly Judy's voice, but the opening "Ya won't believe this" makes the genteel letter-writer coarser than she is.

flow.evidence: Smooth on the whole; the opener "Ya won't believe this, but you never answered my question" is an awkward join.

variety.evidence: Varied terms, but the sign-off repeats: "Hooroo, Daddy" and then "Hooroo till January".

essence.evidence: Clearly the same letter with its entries and bells: "(Chapel bell.)", "I have the honour to report fresh explorations".

problems.quote: Ya won't believe this, but you never answered my question
problems.original: You never answered my question and it was very important.
problems.why: Stage-Aussie opener bolted on; out of character for Judy.
"Merry Chrissie" is a forced greeting; Australians say Merry Christmas.
Repeats the Hooroo used a few lines earlier.

B.summary: Faithful and lively, but a little heavier than asked, with a stagey opener and a forced Christmas greeting.

meaning.evidence: Nearly the original word for word, so nothing is lost: "I have it planned exactly what you look like--very satisfactorily", "have your secretary telegraph".

sense.evidence: The few swaps mostly fit ("verandah roof", "heaps of others besides"), but "vacation" became "I’m going to have a beautiful time in holiday", which breaks the phrase.

authenticity.evidence: Little Aussie at all; what is there is spelling ("colour", "realising", "honour") plus a pasted "a merry Chrissie!" and US forms left in: "my nice red bath robe", "Good-by, Daddy".

register.evidence: Largely untranslated: apart from "verandah", "heaps" and "Chrissie", the text is the original ("You’re a snappy old thing with a temper."), lighter than a level-2 brief.

tone.evidence: Being the original, the tone is whole: "Oh, you see, I know! You’re a snappy old thing with a temper."

flow.evidence: The original prose reads well, but the swap "a beautiful time in holiday" is ungrammatical.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original: "(Ten o’clock bell. This is a very interrupted letter.)"

problems.quote: I’m going to have a beautiful time in holiday
problems.original: I’m going to have a beautiful time in vacation
problems.why: Word swap broke the grammar; Australians say "over the holidays".

problems.quote: You’re a snappy old thing with a temper.
problems.original: You’re a snappy old thing with a temper.
problems.why: Representative of the whole: the text is left largely untranslated against a level-2 brief.

C.summary: Essentially the original with spelling changes and a couple of swaps, one of which breaks the grammar; far too light for the brief.
